questions.prompt: EduOps is described as a modular monolith. Explain how its code is split and why path aliases are used, state the one dependency rule not to break and what it buys, what to do when a rule function seems to need the database, and why the @/db client is kept as a singleton on globalThis in development.

keyPoints.text: It ships as one Next.js app, but the code is split into five virtual packages under src/packages, each with its own TypeScript path alias.
keyPoints.quote: Everything ships as one Next.js app, but the code is split into five *virtual packages*

keyPoints.text: The aliases exist to make illegal imports feel wrong.
keyPoints.quote: The aliases exist to make illegal imports feel wrong

keyPoints.text: @/domain imports nothing: no Prisma, no Next.js, no logger; it takes plain numbers and strings and returns plain objects.
keyPoints.quote: No Prisma, no Next.js, no logger.

keyPoints.text: That makes domain rules trivially unit-testable.
keyPoints.quote: That is what makes it trivially unit-testable

keyPoints.text: It also lets the same grade formula be called from a page, a Server Action, a background job and an agent without diverging.
keyPoints.quote:
the same grade formula can be called from a page, a Server Action, a
background job, and an agent without any of them diverging.

keyPoints.text: Everything else may depend on @/domain, but @/domain may depend on nothing else.
keyPoints.quote:
Nothing in `@/domain` may depend on anything
else.

keyPoints.text: If a rule seems to need a query, fetch in the caller and pass the facts in.
keyPoints.quote:
the fix
is to fetch in the caller and pass the facts in

keyPoints.text: The Prisma client is stashed on globalThis in development because hot-reload re-evaluates modules and would otherwise open a new SQLite connection on every save.
keyPoints.quote:
Next.js hot-reload re-evaluates modules and would otherwise open a new SQLite connection
on every save until the process dies.

questions.prompt: Explain EduOps' observability package for logging and auditing: where a log call writes, how generateFingerprint turns messages into a grouping key and why that is useful, what happens when the log's database write fails, what an audit event records, and what the audit helper does when its own insert throws (and the trade-off that represents).

keyPoints.text: A logger call writes to the console and also inserts a SystemLog row (debug is the exception: it writes nothing in production).
keyPoints.quote:
Every call
  writes to `console` *and* inserts a `SystemLog` row.

keyPoints.text: generateFingerprint lowercases the message and replaces UUIDs, emails and long numbers with placeholders, then prefixes the service name.
keyPoints.quote:
it lowercases the message and replaces UUIDs, emails
  and long numbers

keyPoints.text: The result is a stable grouping key, so the same error 400 times collapses to one signature.
keyPoints.quote: That gives you a stable grouping key

keyPoints.text: Log DB write failures are swallowed so logging can never break a request.
keyPoints.quote: DB write failures are swallowed so logging can never break a request.

keyPoints.text: recordAuditEvent writes an AuditEvent with JSON-stringified before/after snapshots, then emits an info log.
keyPoints.quote: writes an `AuditEvent` with `JSON.stringify`'d before/after snapshots

keyPoints.text: Auditing is fail-open: if the audit insert throws, the error is logged and the caller continues.
keyPoints.quote:
if the audit insert throws, the error is logged and the
  caller continues.

keyPoints.text: That is a deliberate choice of availability over auditability, worth arguing about in a design review.
keyPoints.quote: availability over auditability

questions.prompt: Walk through the contract of EduOps' agent orchestrator, executeAgentRun: what it records before doing any work and why, how it gathers and records what the agent knew, what the registry functions are allowed to do, what happens on success and on a throw, why every agent shares one output shape, and how an agent is honest about missing data.

keyPoints.text: It inserts an AgentRun row with status Pending before any work, so a crash still leaves a trace.
keyPoints.quote:
so a crash
   still leaves a trace.

keyPoints.text: It loads exactly the facts each agent needs and rejects a mismatched target type.
keyPoints.quote:
to load exactly the facts that agent needs, and validate the
   target type matches

keyPoints.text: The plain-JSON agentInput is the "prompt"; it is saved to inputSnapshotJSON (with the successful result) so you can later see precisely what the agent knew.
keyPoints.quote:
It is snapshotted
   into `inputSnapshotJSON` so you can later see precisely what the agent knew.

keyPoints.text: Registry functions are pure, (input) => { output, trace }, and never touch the database.
keyPoints.quote: They never touch the database.

keyPoints.text: On success it persists Succeeded with output, confidence and trace, plus an audit event and a log.
keyPoints.quote: Persist `Succeeded` with the output, confidence, and trace; write an audit event and a log.

keyPoints.text: On a throw it persists Failed and returns the run id instead of rethrowing, because a failed analysis must not 500 the page.
keyPoints.quote: a failed analysis must not 500 the page.

keyPoints.text: A uniform AgentOutput shape lets one component render any agent's result, so a new agent must not invent a new shape.
keyPoints.quote: If you add an agent, do not invent a new output shape.

keyPoints.text: The limitations array plus a reduced confidenceScore is the honesty mechanism instead of silent guessing.
keyPoints.quote: The `limitations` array plus a reduced `confidenceScore` is the honesty mechanism
